intro: The startup pivoted eleven times in one quarter, and the last pivot left a trail of cryptic commit messages and a whiteboard nobody is allowed to erase. The engineering team keeps a long drawer of spare keycaps and blank badge reels under the bench by the rack; each cubby in the foam insert was carved to fit one exact part, and when a new component arrives, someone spends an evening with a hot knife until the foam holds it perfectly. Nobody has drawn on the whiteboard since the eleventh pivot; the markers have dried out in their trays. The drawer has no labels, but everyone knows which cubby a bent bracket belongs in.
echo: The investors are hunting for a mythical beast worth a billion.

puzzles.title: Monday Deploy
puzzles.flavor: A light on the far shore that refuses to stay on.
hints: Only two kinds of mark, in groups of one to four. Which old alphabet is built from exactly that?
Morse code: one mark is a dot, the other a dash. Try it both ways round.

puzzles.title: Blameless
puzzles.flavor: Arms out, arms up, arms down: a dance with no music.
hints: Imagine each of these as a person holding two flags out at arm's length. Sailors had an alphabet for that.
Flag semaphore: the two hands are the two arms, and each pair of angles is a letter.

puzzles.title: Standup
puzzles.flavor: Walk the fence; don't read it.

blocks.text: IYUAR ATISN ECTEY UAELE DFUDH ASEWI HSPIT FOCNE DHSET NEHNO HVARA YONTE NWRHC ISRN

hints: All the right letters are here, just out of order. Could they have been written along a path that goes up and down?
Rail fence: written in a zigzag over a few rows, then copied out row by row. Try two to five rows.

puzzles.title: Offsite
puzzles.flavor: The clerk ran out of alphabet and kept going anyway.
hints: Which short words are most common in English? Could any of them be hiding here?
Each symbol always stands for the same letter. The finished sentence tells you what to submit.

puzzles.title: Runway
puzzles.flavor: Around the edges first; the point comes last.
hints: All the letters of a sentence are here, but not in rows. Try walking the grid the way a snail would.
Start in one corner and spiral inward along the edges; one corner and one direction read as a sentence.

puzzles.title: Hockey Stick
puzzles.flavor: Everything came out of the wash with a little something extra.
hints: Each jumble is almost a word from this round, but with a letter to spare. Which letter, every time?
Rearrange each into a theme word; the spare letters, in order, are the answer.

puzzles.title: Postmortem
puzzles.flavor: The radio operator had everything back to front, but only from A to Z.
hints: Each word stands for a letter, the way radio operators spell. Do those letters read? If not, try the alphabet backwards.
Take the NATO call signs' initials, then swap each letter for its mirror: A for Z, B for Y.

meta.title: Meta: Series Z
meta.flavor: Everything at the office has a place.
hints: The grid's rows are all different lengths. So are your answers.
Put each answer in the row its length fits; read the shaded squares top to bottom.
